The logs confirm the reported figures. The run has now completed with full-file readback after remount, and its receipt records the E70 image retained. Seq and dd each issued 67 erase commands, with average erase guard spans of about 2.29 ms and 2.98 ms. I’m checking how allocation and the earlier workload could explain that difference; the logs contain no pre-erase content or sector-address trace.

The frozen LittleFS source makes allocation history a plausible explanation: “free” means unreferenced, not necessarily erased, and new COW blocks are erased before use. Remounting also changes the allocation starting point using a metadata-derived seed. Repeating a filename therefore cannot guarantee reuse of the same sectors.

One WEL-status-reuse build is worth measuring before pursuing 256-byte PP. It targets the roughly 304–308 ms program cost in these phases. The dd result needs about 38 ms to reach 500 KiB/s on its original timing basis, but that saving—and the full durable timing—still needs measurement.

The frozen image already enables NSH’s `time` command. Its source times a foreground command through return, including close, so root can add a coarse whole-command measurement without a firmware change. It still uses the 10 ms clock; results near 512 ms would need finer timing before a durable-throughput claim.

I’ll review the completed WEL capture, verify its measurements and firmware pairing, and compare program cost with E73’s history-repeat run. Then I’ll recommend one bounded FS experiment in the new result-review file.

The capture records both verified passes and UART release. All four whole-command times exceed 512 ms, so the fastest inner rates do not establish sustained 500 KiB/s. I’m checking the raw counter deltas to separate program-cost savings from erase variation.

WEL’s program guard spans are 25.4–29.5 ms lower per workload than E73’s, an observed 8.1–9.6% reduction. Erase spans differ by 293–521 ms, so they account for most of the overall speedup; the separate boots prevent a controlled causal comparison. All four raw 262144-byte readbacks match exactly. Kmem remains 3552 bytes above baseline after quiet, while pages, IOBs, tasks and live address environments return to their baseline counts.

The counter checks pass for all eight WEL snapshots and all fourteen earlier E73 snapshots, with migration zero. WEL still inherits the partial-read formatter defect, so arithmetic agreement supports these Flash deltas without proving the whole report atomic.

I recommend a bounded feasibility probe for true 256-byte programming next. It must first establish safe SPI1 completion with CS held across 64-byte segments, then measure the actual page-cost reduction. Program-only savings cannot cover the older slow histories if their measured erase costs recur.

Completed [result-review.md](/home/regex/work/esp32s31-openvela/backups/xts-adaptation-and-test-evidence/korvo-fs-wel-status-reuse/result-review.md).

- All four full payload readbacks match exactly. Firmware pairing and Flash counter arithmetic check out; the formatter’s atomicity limitation remains.
- Whole-command rates are **426.7/376.5**, then **465.5/449.1 KiB/s**. None meets 500.
- Program spans are **8.1–9.6% lower** than E73’s, but much larger erase differences dominate overall improvement. This is not controlled A/B evidence.
- Kmem remains **+3552 bytes**; pages, IOBs, tasks and live address-environment counts return to baseline.

**Next:** one bounded feasibility probe for genuine 256-byte PP: first prove safe SPI1 continuation/completion/recovery, then measure actual program savings on owned scratch space. No nominal HAL-size change or global geometry change.
